title: 4 ‘Strong Buy’ REITs That Should Outperform

&l;p&g;&l;a href=&q;https://blogs.forbes.com/bradthomas/files/2018/03/upq.jpg&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;&l;img class=&q;size-medium wp-image-2920&q; src=&q;http://blogs-images.forbes.com/bradthomas/files/2018/03/upq-300×186.jpg?width=960&q; alt=&q;&q; data-height=&q;186&q; data-width=&q;300&q;&g;&l;/a&g; Source: Pexels 
Some analysts use the term &q;strong buy&q;&a;nbsp;to get page views or excite readers, but I consider a strong buy to mean the following: 
&l;/p&g;&l;blockquote&g;&l;strong&g;&a;ldquo;Strong Buy&l;/strong&g;&a;nbsp;means that I am recommending a high-quality REIT that is trading at a wider margin of safety. Recognizing principal preservation is critical, my recommendation is telegraphing readers that the company is a blue chip on sale.&a;rdquo;&l;/blockquote&g; 
In my monthly newsletter (&l;em&g;Forbes&l;/em&g; Real Estate Investor) I have labeled six REITs as strong buys and I just upgraded two others (as &l;span&g;strong buy&l;/span&g;s). As we enter 2018, most analysts have suspected that the fear of rising rates had already been priced in and nobody (including me) suspected that there would be an extreme February selloff in REIT-land. 
After all, REITs were exhibiting strong earnings and dividend growth performance and there was really no reason to suspect Mr. Market would spook the crowd once again. However, Ben Graham provides us with some direction: 
&a;ldquo;Experience teaches that the time to buy stocks is when their price is unduly depressed by temporary adversity. In other words, they should be bought on a bargain basis or not at all.&a;rdquo; 
As Thomas Bohjalian, CFA, executive vice president at Cohen &a;amp; Steers,&a;nbsp;&l;a href=&q;https://www.cohenandsteers.com/insights/read/rate-reaction-opens-a-reit-opportunity-us&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;explains&l;/a&g;: 
&l;blockquote&g;&a;ldquo;One of the things we find that some investors and the financial press consistently get wrong about REITs is the relationship with interest rates&a;mdash; that if rates are rising, you shouldn&a;rsquo;t own REITs. This belief, however disconnected from historical evidence, often seems too ingrained to suggest otherwise. 
Interest rates are part of the equation, and sudden moves in bond yields can create volatility. But REITs are not bonds. In an improving economy, landlords can raise rents as tenants fight for more space, potentially increasing cash flows to offset the effects of higher rates. In other words, it should matter why rates are rising, not simply that rates are rising&a;hellip;. 
While we cannot say when REITs will reverse their recent underperformance. We see this as an attractive opportunity to begin legging into higher REIT allocations , taking advantage of low relative valuations, strong diversification potential and robust demand in the private market.&a;rdquo;&l;/blockquote&g; 
&l;strong&g;4 REITs That Should Outperform&l;/strong&g; 
As I said, I now have eight&a;nbsp;&l;span&g;strong buy&l;/span&g;s included in the &l;em&g;Forbes&l;/em&g; Real Estate Investor (monthly newsletter) and today I am going to provide an overview of four my favorites: 
&l;strong&g;Simon Property Group&l;/strong&g; (SPG) is a dominating mall REIT that recently increased its quarterly dividend to $1.95 from $1.85, up 5%, and it is the company&s;s third consecutive quarterly dividend increase. This sends a strong signal to Simon investors that there is a true alignment of interest and that the dividend is safe and growing. 
Simon has grown its annual dividend by approximately 15%, the highest growth in the mall REIT sector. The company&s;s dividend growth is supported by the conservative balance sheet and reasonable payout ratio. 
Following a 33% reduction in the common dividend from the 2008 level, Simon has returned to its historical pattern of regular dividend increases. The dividend is a priority for Simon and the company should continue to increase it by 5% over the long term. 
Simon has dominating market share that includes ownership interests in over 230 retail properties totaling over 190 million square feet located across North America and Asia. Additionally, the company has an expanding footprint in Europe with its 29% interest in Klepierre&a;nbsp;(a leading European mall operator based in France) and a joint venture with McArthurGlen (a leader in European designer outlets). 
Simon offers REIT investors a very compelling opportunity to own shares in trophy – the company owns primarily &q;A&q; malls which have higher sales productivity and are in better locations than the B and C malls. The long-term outlook for the A malls is favorable and Simon&s;s fortress balance should allow the company to continue to generate steady and reliable dividends; after all, &q;&l;em&g;the safest dividend is the one that&s;s just been raised.&l;/em&g;&q; 
&l;a href=&q;https://blogs.forbes.com/bradthomas/files/2018/03/spg.jpg&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;&l;img class=&q;size-medium wp-image-2916&q; src=&q;http://blogs-images.forbes.com/bradthomas/files/2018/03/spg-300×234.jpg?width=960&q; alt=&q;&q; data-height=&q;234&q; data-width=&q;300&q;&g;&l;/a&g; Source: FAST Graphs 
&l;strong&g;LTC Properties&l;/strong&g; (LTC) dividend yield has breached 6%, the company has maintained very consistent record of increasing dividends. LTC has raised its dividend every year except 2009 (when the company just froze the payout and did not cut the dividend). 
LTC is a healthcare REIT that has been around for over 25 years; the company was incorporated on May 12, 1992, in the state of Maryland, and commenced operations on August 25, 1992. It invests primarily in senior housing and long-term healthcare property types, including skilled nursing properties (50.8%), assisted living properties (46.9%), independent living properties and combinations thereof. 
&l;!–nextpage–&g; 
LTC owns a portfolio of 201 properties, three development projects and four land parcels (in 29 states), that includes a well-balanced geographic footprint. Texas has the highest concentration (17.1%), followed by Michigan (14.1%) and Wisconsin (8.0%). 
Historically LTC has grown its dividend by around 5% per year and the estimate for 2018 is just under 4%. The company has maintained a consistent payout ratio of 80% (based on AFFO) and this REIT is one of the most predictable monthly dividend payers and shares are now yielding 6.0%. 
&l;a href=&q;https://blogs.forbes.com/bradthomas/files/2018/03/ltc.jpg&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;&l;img class=&q;size-medium wp-image-2917&q; src=&q;http://blogs-images.forbes.com/bradthomas/files/2018/03/ltc-300×233.jpg?width=960&q; alt=&q;&q; data-height=&q;233&q; data-width=&q;300&q;&g;&l;/a&g; Source: FAST Graphs 
&l;strong&g;Tanger Factory Outlets&l;/strong&g; (SKT) is the only publicly-traded REIT specializing solely in the development, leasing, marketing and operations of outlet centers in the United States and Canada. The company owns 44 outlet centers in the U.S. (22 states) and Canada. 
Since pioneering the dynamic outlet industry in 1981, Tanger remains an industry leader that strives to provide superior experience to consumers, retail-partners and shareholders. 
To maintain a strong and flexible leverage profile, Tanger prefers to use internally generated cash to fund any further purchases under the share repurchase program. The redemption make-whole premium and the completion of the two projects that will open later this year will consume the remaining cash flow for the balance of the year. 
At Q3-17, Tanger&a;rsquo;s AFFO available to common shareholders per share increased 2.3% compared to the prior-year period. AFFO available to common shareholders was $179.7 million, or $1.80 per share, for the 2017 period and $177.5 million, or $1.76 per share, for the 2016 period. 
Tanger continues to expand its tenant base providing sound traffic growth enhancement, that in turn, should restore tenant sales and grow beyond $400 per square foot. Also, as previously referenced, tax reform should also serve as a catalyst and this is effective in 2018. 
&l;a href=&q;https://blogs.forbes.com/bradthomas/files/2018/03/skt.jpg&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;&l;img class=&q;size-medium wp-image-2918&q; src=&q;http://blogs-images.forbes.com/bradthomas/files/2018/03/skt-300×234.jpg?width=960&q; alt=&q;&q; data-height=&q;234&q; data-width=&q;300&q;&g;&l;/a&g; Source: FAST Graphs 
&l;strong&g;Physicians Realty&l;/strong&g; (DOC) is a new edition to the &l;span&g;strong buy&l;/span&g; basket, shares have fallen by over 17% year-to-date, creating a wider margin of safety for value investors. 
The company exploded out of the gate, having completed its IPO, and more recently closing on the $700 million Catholic Health Initiatives portfolio acquisition, and new investments in 2016 ($1.3 billion) and 2017 (nearly $1.4 billion). 
Physicians Realty owns 14 million square feet that is 96.6% leased, with over 50% of that space leased directly to investment grade rated healthcare systems and their subsidiaries. During 2017 the weighted average age of DOC&a;rsquo;s building improved from 20 years to 18 years and the average size of facilities increased from 44,000 feet to 50,000 feet. 
The company&a;rsquo;s normalized funds available for distribution (or FAD) was $44.2 million, or $0.24 per share in Q4-17. For the full year of 2017 the normalized FFO per share was $1.04, representing a 6% increase over the comparable period last year. 
Physicians Realty is now yielding 6.2% and I consider that highly attractive, especially when you consider the enhanced credit quality of the portfolio. I am especially glad to see the company continuing to reduce its Payout Ratio, signaling that a dividend increase could be soon (late 2018 or early 2019). 
&l;a href=&q;https://blogs.forbes.com/bradthomas/files/2018/03/doc1.jpg&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;&l;img class=&q;size-medium wp-image-2919&q; src=&q;http://blogs-images.forbes.com/bradthomas/files/2018/03/doc1-300×234.jpg?width=960&q; alt=&q;&q; data-height=&q;234&q; data-width=&q;300&q;&g;&l;/a&g; Source: FAST Graphs 
I own shares in SPG, LTC, SKT, and DOC.
